extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants (patent prosecution audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, determining scope/content/analogy of prior art, and handling applicant replies and rebuttal evidence during patent prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales supporting obviousness (exemplary list A–G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include several articulated bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List (A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results; (B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results; (C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way; (D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results; (E) “Obvious to try” – choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success; (F) Known work in one field may prompt predictable variations in same or different field based on design incentives/market forces; (G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify or combine teachings to arrive at the claimed invention. See MPEP §2143 and §2144–§2144.09 for examples and additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to clearly articulate reasons for a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be some articulated reasoning with rational underpinning (KSR citing In re Kahn). The analysis supporting a 103 rejection should be made explicit and the Office action should clearly communicate findings and how conclusions are supported by facts. Office personnel should consider multiple rationales and explicitly state the rationale relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply obligations under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must distinctly and specifically point out supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence is not substantively adequate. See MPEP §706.07(a) for consequences (examiner may repeat rejection and make next action final).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traverse of factual findings must be reasoned and substantive
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the Office erred substantively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere assertions are insufficient; the traverse should explain the specific factual error(s). If applicant fails to substantively rebut factual findings, the examiner may sustain and make final the rejection under MPEP §706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant's rebuttal evidence (secondary considerations and unexpected results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include 'secondary considerations' such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and evidence of unexpected results (citing Graham). After rebuttal is presented, examiners must reconsider the obviousness determination in view of the entire record and articulate how conclusions change or remain. Examples of applicant evidence for combination claims include: (A) inability to combine by known methods due to technological difficulties; (B) combination elements do not merely perform their separate functions; (C) claimed combination produced unexpected results. See MPEP §2145 and §716–§716.10 regarding affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art available under 35 U.S.C. 102 may be used under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art may be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of whether it otherwise qualifies under statutory categories of 102. A 103 rejection is based on underlying 102 categories depending on publication/issue dates (e.g., a patent issued >1 year before filing can be treated like a 102(b) bar). Affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 may be used to swear behind a reference. See MPEP §§901–901.06(d), §§2121–2129 and §2129 for admissions as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of the prior art must be evaluated as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers must 'cast the mind back' to the time of invention and not use knowledge of the claimed invention to interpret prior art. See MPEP §2145 paragraph X.A. and the cited case law (W.L. Gore v. Garlock). Examiners should avoid hindsight reasoning when articulating rationale for combining references.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — burden and evidence to show disqualification of certain prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant seeking benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that subject matter qualifying as prior art only under 102(e),(f),(g) was owned by or subject to assignment to the same person at the time the invention was made, or that joint research agreement conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant bears the burden to show: (A) claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention resulted from activities within scope of the joint research agreement; (C) application discloses or is amended to disclose names of parties to the agreement. For common ownership evidence and JRAs see MPEP §706.02(l)(2) and related case law (e.g., Ex parte Yoshino, In re Bartfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for use of a reference in a 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem. Examiner should consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support analogy. See Bigio, KSR, In re Icon Health, In re Clay, and In re Klein decisions; see MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider similarities and differences in structure and function when assessing analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry significant weight in determining whether references are analogous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification and cross-references are some evidence, but courts place greater weight on structural and functional similarities (e.g., In re Ellis). Examiner should evaluate whether the reference's structure/function overlap makes it pertinent to the inventor's problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art considerations across different arts (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific considerations and precedent exist for analogy in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical arts: teachings across carrier/absorbent/dye arts may be pertinent if problem is chemical in nature (Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, In re Mlot-Fijalkowski). Mechanical arts: broad prior art exploration is often reasonable where similar problems exist (Stevenson; In re Bigio; In re Deminski). Electrical arts: designers look to solutions for analogous problems like rate-limiting (Medtronic). Design arts: a prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use; examples and MPEP §1504.03 provide further guidance (In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera). These precedents illustrate how art-specific facts inform analogy analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both invention and prior art references as a whole. Case law (Stratoflex, Schenck, In re Hirao) shows that admitted unobvious aspects of a multi-part claim can render the subject matter as a whole nonobvious. Examiners should avoid isolating individual differences and must weigh the combined contribution of claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill an invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' that disregards the 'as a whole' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing an invention to a single gist or thrust and ignoring express claim limitations violates the 'as a whole' analysis required under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind) demonstrate that focusing on a single conceptual insight while ignoring express limitations can lead to improper obviousness findings. Examiners must analyze all claimed limitations and not treat claims as though they read differently than written.
